author: John Jefferson Tan
title: "He could not defend Stockton-to-Malone on that play" - Lakers journalist blames Shaquille O'Neal because Utah dominated L.A. in the '90s - NewsBreak
text: Shaquille O'Neal was expected to be the driving force that would lead the Los Angeles Lakers back to championship glory. However, in his first few years with the team, the Lakers faced significant challenges, particularly during their matchups against the Utah Jazz in the playoffs. According to Lakers journalist and author Jeff Pearlman, Shaq played a pivotal role in the Lakers' inability to overcome the Jazz. He argued that the Lakers consistently struggled to find an effective strategy against the dynamic duo of Karl Malone and John Stockton. Based on Pearlman's assessment, it was O'Neal's responsibility to counter Malone and Stockton's impact on the game. Unfortunately, despite his overwhelming size and power, he lacked the defensive prowess needed to stop the Jazz tandem throughout those series. "A big part of it was Shaq was an awful pick-and-roll defender," Pearlman told Hoops Analyst in 2020. "Brutally bad. Maybe, one of the worst pick-and-roll defenders of that era. He could not defend Stockton-to-Malone on that play. The one thing you had to do was defend that play, or Utah would do it to death on you." Shaq's defensive shortcoming ultimately proved detrimental to the Lakers' championship aspirations. As a result, the team found themselves unable to advance past the Jazz , a pattern that haunted them for years. Apart from O'Neal's inability to be a force on the defensive end, inexperience was also one of the main reasons why the Lakers struggled against the Jazz in the '90s. Pearlman pointed out that chemistry was a significant distinction between the Jazz and the Lakers during their playoff encounters. He reckoned that Utah exhibited a level of cohesion that was evidently superior to that of L.A. Unlike the young and careless Lakers, the Jazz approached the game with a calculated and systematic strategy. Furthermore, Pearlman emphasized that Utah's success was not solely dependent on their star players, Stockton and Malone. Instead, the team was also bolstered by several key role players who stepped up and consistently challenged the Lakers. "The Lakers were outgunned. Utah was better coached," Pearlman weighed in. "Stockton and Malone were still kind of at their peaks and were marvelous players. They had a great system. Also, not for nothing, but Greg Ostertag, an otherwise forgettable name in NBA history, played Shaq well. He was big and goony and strong. [Ostertag] was not graceful, but he beat the hell out of you." "Utah was better," he pointed out. "It's like why Detroit beat the Bulls until Jordan figured it out. It wasn't quite the Lakers' time yet and the Jazz were a really good team," Pearlman concluded. The Lakers didn't expect a lot from Kobe Bryant at the time compared to O'Neal due to his age. However, it would've been great if the teenager managed to significantly contribute to the team during their playoff battles with the Jazz. Bryant's infamous airball party during the 1997 playoffs serves as a poignant illustration of how young and unprepared the Lakers were at that time. Pearlman revealed that the Jazz recognized that they had the Lakers exactly where they wanted them to be when Kobe shot those awful airballs. "The game in 1996-97 where Kobe put up the air balls really fascinated me," Pearlman admitted. "I talked to a lot of guys on the Utah bench and they said all they wanted was for Kobe to shoot. This was the best thing ever. They had Eddie Jones and Nick Van Exel standing there and you're going to give the ball to this 18-year-old kid to shoot air balls. I tried really hard to find the last time an NBA player shot four air balls in a game and I couldn't find it anywhere." Related: "We only needed one more guy" - Patrick Beverley says the Clippers lost SGA because Kawhi thought he needed more help Though O'Neal failed to lead the Lakers against the Jazz, he understood that it was his role as a leader to uplift his teammates. Following Kobe's air ball party , Shaq comforted his young co-star and reassured him that it would never define his career. "Look at all these people laughing at you. One day we're gonna get them back," Jack MacMullan recalled Shaq's message to Kobe on "The Icons Club." "Don't worry, someday everyone is gonna be screaming your name. Take this and learn from it." The Lakers lost to the Jazz in back-to-back postseasons. The two teams did not meet in the playoffs in 1999 in what could've been a third showdown. However, the Lakers suffered another devastating playoff elimination at the hands of the eventual NBA champions, the San Antonio Spurs, in the Western Conference semifinals. The following season, the Lakers brought in Phil Jackson, the legendary coach who beat the Jazz in the Finals twice. With him at the helm, Shaq and Kobe finally hit their stride. Though they never crossed paths with the Jazz again in the playoffs, the Lakers established themselves as the best team in the league.
